messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
I am analyzing data on seabirds in the Baltic Sea. Counting is carried out from a ship on 42 linear transects, each transect is divided into segments (approximately the same length). I carried out dozens of simulations using various models and various databases.
Creating a database structure I divided the transects into segments, added subsection - segments to the database, at the 'observation' level, there are data about perpendicular distance and cluster sizes.
I would like to ask, what type of analysis will be most relevant to this type of data? As a default in the Distance software on the CDS model is the Half-normal Cosine function. I conducted an analysis of this model and the results seem real. The icon next to the result of the analysis, however, is displayed in orange indicating a few warnings:
** Warning: The number of adjustment parameters allowed has been reduced to   2 because of a limited number of intervals. **
** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **
** Warning: Exact distance values, rather than distance intervals, have been used in size bias regression calculations. **
Do these warnings have any significant impact? I would ask for advice on what basis to choose the best model and how to justify this? Is the default Half-normal Cosine function the best for this type of data and if so why?
I made many trials with different CDS models, I also tried the MCDS model, where I used cluster size as a covariate. Even in one simulation (MCDS), a green icon appeared next to the result, without any warnings. I wonder just why in MCDS results there is no 95% CI in the estimate of density results (D)?
And the last question is why a strange number appears at N (estimate of the number of animals), how to decipher it, eg: N=0.57034E+06
All the best,
Dominik
PS. Attached, I am sending a sample of my database, there are two additional columns: sea state and depth, which I did not use in the analysis.

Dominik:  thanks for your questions and I'm grateful to Jochen for offering his assistance.  Let me comment on a couple of technical details.

When Distance for Windows issues warnings, the meaning is that the software is trying to follow two sets of instructions that are in conflict.

Warning 1: seems you have created bin intervals for your perpendicular distances.  The number of "points of support" in your data is equal to the number of bins.  Distance will not fit a model with more parameters than points of support, even though a model with more parameters would produce a better fit to the data.

Warning 2: the premise behind distance sampling is that probability of detection declines smoothly at increasing distances from the transect.  Because of random variation in the observation process, the histograms of perpendicular distances are not necessarily continuously decreasing.  The software is faced with a paradox:  produce the best fit to the data (which would require the detection function increase over some range of distances) or be consistent with the premise of using models that produce smooth decreases.  The message is that the software has chosen the latter.

Warning 3: even though you have binned your distances for the purpose of fitting the detection function, the software has used the original exact distances when performing the size bias regression correction.

With regard to the way the software presents the estimate of abundance, this is called scientific notation.  The number to the right of the "E" in this case "+06" indicates the decimal point of the remainder of the number "0.57034" should be moved "6" to the right, making the resulting number 570340; i.e. just over half a million birds.

I'll let you and Jochen have a discussion about other issues.  Thanks again Jochen.

Eric Rexstad

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm going to use Distance to analyze point transect data, which I have never done before (have only done line transects in the past). I want to make sure I'm on the right track when it comes to entering data into Distance for this purpose. I have included a screenshot of some sample data below, for reference.

In my example, I have named my transects gs-001, gs-002, and gs-003. Each of these transects consists of points, spaced 100 m apart, from which biologists conduct surveys. My first question is, should I be listing the actual transects here, as I have, or should I be listing the individual points?

Second question: We visited each transect three times, so is it okay to have the survey effort be '3'? I'm thinking that if I leave it as '1,' I would then have to use a multiplier somewhere down the line?

Radial distance seems straightforward, but my final question is this: What if someone detected the same individual of a target species from more than one point along the transect? For example, they saw a hawk perched on a post when they were at the first point along the transect, and the hawk was still there when the observer arrived at the second point along the transect. That would only get recorded once per line transect, of course, and could be recorded more than once if seen from multiple line transects, but I'm wondering how this is dealt with for point transects?

Thanks in advance, I always appreciate everyone's expertise in this forum.

Best,
Nick Peterson

Nick

Nice to hear from you again.  Short answers to some of your questions:
your data set-up is correct.  The sampling unit is the point; the transects are merely a way of getting from one to the next; no sampling is taking place while in transit.  Hence it need not be reflected in your data organisation..
Representing effort as the number of visits is just right and does avoid the need for a multiplier.  Another advantage of using the effort field rather than a multiplier is that gives flexibility should not all points be visited an equal number of times (if there were fewer crew available for a visit or if a pesky bear prevents visits to some points on a scheduled visit).
Detections of an individual from multiple points might be thought to cause problems.  The situation you describe, where you know it is the same individual, probably best to only record the first detection.  The situation is probably more subtle--detections are made by sound, how to know if it is the same individual? I draw your attention to the 2006 Auk paper by Prof. Buckland in which he conducted a simulation study to examine exactly this situation:
Buckland, Stephen T. 2006. Point-transect surveys for songbirds: robust methodologies. The Auk 123 (2): 345–57. Dominik:  thanks for your questions and I'm grateful to Jochen for offering his assistance.  Let me comment on a couple of technical details.

When Distance for Windows issues warnings, the meaning is that the software is trying to follow two sets of instructions that are in conflict.

Warning 1: seems you have created bin intervals for your perpendicular distances.  The number of "points of support" in your data is equal to the number of bins.  Distance will not fit a model with more parameters than points of support, even though a model with more parameters would produce a better fit to the data.

Warning 2: the premise behind distance sampling is that probability of detection declines smoothly at increasing distances from the transect.  Because of random variation in the observation process, the histograms of perpendicular distances are not necessarily continuously decreasing.  The software is faced with a paradox:  produce the best fit to the data (which would require the detection function increase over some range of distances) or be consistent with the premise of using models that produce smooth decreases.  The message is that the software has chosen the latter.

Warning 3: even though you have binned your distances for the purpose of fitting the detection function, the software has used the original exact distances when performing the size bias regression correction.

With regard to the way the software presents the estimate of abundance, this is called scientific notation.  The number to the right of the "E" in this case "+06" indicates the decimal point of the remainder of the number "0.57034" should be moved "6" to the right, making the resulting number 570340; i.e. just over half a million birds.

Hello.

While validating a python program for automating Distance Sampling analyses through MCDS.exe R6.2,
we've encountered a few strange cases linked sightings order in input data files for MCDS.exe.

Let me explain one of these cases :
* from the same point transect sample (Turdus merula sightings in Auvergne, France, april to june, 2019),
* we ran the same simple CDS analyses with Half-normal Cosine and Uniform Cosine models
  (nothing else special, no distance truncation, ...) :

  1) through Distance 7.3 software,
  2) through direct use of MCDS.exe command line.
        $ cd <into the data.txt + cmd.txt folder>
        $ "C:\Program Files (x86)\Distance 7\MCDS.exe" 0, cmd.txt

For these analyses, when comparing method 1 and 2, the results were :
* rigourously identical for the Half-normal Cosine,
* quite different for the Uniform Cosine model, with quite same AIC, but double / half estimate density (!).

After investigating, it appears that :
1) Distance 7.3 (under Windows 7) has slightly changed the order of imported sightings before calling MCDS.exe :
   the sightings were still sorted by point, but for some points, they were no more in the order of the original
   data file imported into Distance ;
   the order change was systematic, whatever model, Uniform Cosine or Half-normal Cosine, whatever analysis execution ;
   and subsequent re-runs (after cleanup) of the same analyses, or subsequent tries to rebuild the Distance projects
   from scratch ... didn't change anything : always the same order change and results.
   Note: To access the data passed to MCDS.exe, we activated the data logging, and also the Debug mode.
2) MCDS.exe produced different results for the same input data set and Uniform Cosine analysis model,
   when the sigthings were not in the same order (but still sorted by point) ;
   but the results remained the same whatever method for the Half-normal Cosine model.

Isn't this sensitivy to data order some kind of bug or weakness of MCDS.exe ?

Is this simply due to a "bad quality" of our sample that makes the Uniform Cosine model fitting not / pourly applicable ?
(hence the computation warning : ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **)

What is you recommandation as a workaround for this, if any :
* change data order ? (as here, a sort by increasing distance inside each point seems to improve things)
* anything else ?

For reference, you'll find attached a zip archive with the following :
* file "dist-order-sens.xlsx" : the results of 3 analyses run with the same sample data for the Uniform Cosine model,
  1 analysis per line :
  - case "dist-win7-dist-order" : run with Distance 7.3 (method 1), results collected by hand in the results window,
  - case "cmd-win7-dist-order" : run directly by command line (method 2), with input data to MCDS.exe
      copied from Distance run (previous line), and results collected by hand in the output.txt file,
  100% identical to the first line,

  and results collected by hand in the output.txt file.
* sub-folder "dist-win7-dist-order" : a reconstructed by hand file set for a MCDS.exe run by Distance 7.3,
  with MCDS.exe input data.txt and cmd.txt (got through Debug mode), and output files log.txt and output.txt
  with contents copied and pasted from Distance analysis result window.
* sub-folder "cmd-win7-dist-order" : run directly by commande line (method 2), with input data to MCDS.exe
  copied from Distance run (previous line), and "natural" output files of MCDS.exe, mainly stats.txt,
  output.txt and log.txt,
* sub-folder "cmd-win7-orig-order" : run directly by commande line (method 2), with input data to MCDS.exe
  generated "by hand", in the same order of the sample data file given to Distance in line 1,
  and "natural" output files of MCDS.exe, mainly stats.txt, output.txt and log.txt.

Dear Melodious warbler

Thanks for your detailed examination of the data set you have provided.  I've not examined the issue of data sorting and its impact upon the mcds optimisation routines.

Instead, thanks to the data you sent along, I've had a look at the data themselves.  Ignoring the fitted curve for the moment, it is clear that there is little information in the data beyond 250-300m:
The fundamental parameter to be estimated from point transect data is h(0); the slope of this PDF at distance 0.  There is virtually no information in detections make at 300m to help in estimating h(0).  That is why truncation plays a role in analysing distance sampling data.  Note from the figure that the fit of the PDF to the data is poor; the great proportion of the detections are in the range 50-150m and the PDF is not fitting that peak.  This is because the optimisation routines are struggling to figure out how to mimic the data in the tail (beyond 300m).  Note the silly hump at 400m where there are no detections.

I reanalysed this data set imposing a reasonable truncation distance; I tried both 250m and 300m; the resulting estimates were virtually identical at those two truncation distances.  In addition, the fit of the PDF to the data was much improved:

The estimate of h(0) from the untruncated data is 0.85807E-04, resulting in an estimate of P=0.09 (only 1 in 10 birds were detected within the 500m radius of the point).  The same quantities assessed from analysis of the  truncated data h(0)=0.14508E-03 and P=0.15.  That 50% increase in P results in a 50% increase in estimated density from 0.29 to 0.46.  The goodness of fit statistics are all quite good for the truncated data (as your eye can deduce by looking at the PDF figure above).

It is difficult to fit PDFs to point transect data; the shape of the detection function at small distances is most critical, but these small distances coincide with small areas around the point where few birds reside.

The fundamental message from this analysis is that exploratory work needs to first be conducted with the data (look at the radial distance histogram) before attempting to fit models.  Rather than worrying about the performance of the optimisation routines and the sorting of distances within transects, a good look at the data will make analysis more straightforward.

Hello,

I would really appreciate some pointers on the project I am currently working on. I have spatial data for a number of species within an ecosystem that have perpendicular distance measurements from the survey trail. I am trying to conduct a resource selection function for each species using environmental variables and latent variables. One such latent variable should take into account the detectability of the different species based on factors that may increase or decrease the probability of the observer seeing them. In the end, the ideal outcome would be a single column with a detection probability given for each combination of covariates including rows where detections were made. So far I am modeling the detection function with the ddf() function in R with different combinations of the following covariates:

Visibility: distance observer can see at 1m height
cloud: %cloud cover
Rain: binary (yes/no=1/0)
VEG: factor variable with 3 veg types (1,2 & 3)
Group1: %cover of veg type 1
Group2: %cover of veg type 1
Group3: %cover of veg type 1
size: number of animals in the herd
**Something to note is that I want to create a single detection function for the entire research area rather than each transect because some species have very few observations

the data set looks like:

head(fxddd[[1]]$data)
  PairID SURVEY VISIBILITY Group1 Group2 Group3 VEG size  distance RAIN observer detected object
1      3     30         95     20      0    142   3  200     108    0        1        1      1
2      3     31         95     20      0    142   3  300     202    0        1        1      2
3      3     36         95     20      0    142   3  200     330    0        1        1      3
4      3      6         95     20      0    142   3   10      54    0        1        1      4
5      3      5         95     20      0    142   3    2     389    0        1        1      5
6      4     31        126      0      0    160   3  400     166    0        1        1      6

Notice that all transect surveys where no detections were made are removed and that the check.data() function has been used to prepare the data for a covariate distance detection function (giving the last 3 columns)

my process for model selection is to first check the best performing key function based on AIC with formula ~1 (no covariates). Nick

You've gotten quite a sophisticated analysis going (complete with scaling of your detection function covariates).  I understand your interest lies only in the detection function; hence your removal of transects without detections (I note for other readers--this is not standard practice when estimating abundance or density).

I note in passing that the histogram of your data raises some concerns; particularly the lack of detections within 35m of the transects; highlighted by the chi-square value of 8 in that first distance band.  That suggests your study animals might be avoiding the tracks or exhibiting evasive movement.  Points for you to consider.

However, to your questions.  I'm not an expert on the use of predict() in the mrds  package.  But the detection probability generated when ESW=FALSE is the probability that an object with the specified covariate values is detected within w  (450m) of the transect, given it is in that covered strip  (the effect of distance is being integrated out).  Notice observations 103-105 in your data set.  They all share the same values of Group1, Group3, VEG and size; but where detected at different distances (405, 92 and 321).  Those three objects all share the same detection probability of 0.459

Dear Eric Rexstad,

Thank you for the detailed and useful response and also for mentioning the problems with the detection function at short distances. Now that I feel I am getting a grasp on the overall method I would like to address this issue. What you suggested is true, buffalo have a tendency to move out of the way of the survey car which has decreased the number of observations in the first distance strip of 35m. These distance bins are automatically assigned by the function ddf() so I have decided to re-bin the data at 50m intervals (using the parameter breaks= in the argument meta.data=) since it is expected the buffalo don't move more than that by the time the surveyors measure their perpendicular distance. This gives much better goodness of fit, especially in the distances closest to the survey line where it is most important.

I have also found some papers addressing this issue by using distance along transect and observation time but I don't have these data and they are much more complex solutions so I would love to know your thoughts on this before diving in. Thanks again for the time in responding!

- Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hello Distance users,

Over the last two years we have been conducting distance surveys
bi-annually to understand our local population of tortoises and this has
yielded some interesting results. There is a bit of discussion on how we
can improve our survey in order to get the most reliable estimates. The
obvious one would be to increase our distances that we cover for our
various habitat types which may be difficult due to terrain. We also
wanted to consider the possibility of repeating transects twice, ether
by having someone follow at a predefined interval, starting at the
opposite side or just repeating the following day. I believe this idea
was briefly mentioned in one of the online videos. After looking though
the distance software (GUI) we are unsure how to prepare our data file
for import and how to tell distance that we have a higher unit of
effort.

If anyone could offer a clue how to do this I would be most appreciative

Regards,
Germano

For line transects, effort is defined as the amount of travel of the
observers.  Hence, if you have 20 transects, each 1 km in length and
they are all walked twice, the total effort of the survey is 20 * 1 * 2
= 40km and each transect as 2km of effort applied to it.  Short answer:
adjust your line effort to reflect multiple transits.

  ---------  -----------  -----------  --------------  ----------------------
      p        0.41914      0.97676E-01      23.30      0.26593      0.66061

create a new data filter for the rare species
enter the P, SE(P) and degrees of freedom from previous analysis in the multipliers fields of the global layer of the project
however, use the division "/" sign as the number of detections will be divided by P.  P < 1, meaning the resulting quotient will be a quantity larger than the number detected--thereby accounting for imperfect detectability
fit a uniform key function with no adjustments to the rare species
the multiplier in Distance will produce an estimate of the number of animals of the rare species

Hi there,

I have conducted single-observer point count surveys for terrestrial birds on islands. Many islands were too small to have multiple point count locations, but I surveyed all points twice. The number of point counts per island ranges from 1 to 31. I tried to keep them ~250 m apart at all times, when possible. I also tried to keep them 50 m from shore, but this was often not possible, which leads to my first question - see below. I have also been truncating point counts at a 50 m radius in preliminary analyses because it's difficult to accurately measure distance beyond this threshold, and because most of our surveys took place more than 50 m from shore...

Many of the islands look sort of like this: (blue = water, green = area not surveyed, yellow = area surveyed when truncating point counts at 50 m).

My questions are:

1.) Is there any way to correct for unequal areas surveyed?

I've tried fitting models both in Distance 7.3 and the R package version of Distance, but I'm not really sure where I can specify this. I've tried including island area as region area, and the area of land within 50 m as effort, but got some pretty wonky results. I've also considered standardizing the effort for this between 0 and 1. For example, if the entire circle overlays with land, that would be 1. If half of it is water, effort would be 0.5. Might that work? If not, do I just have to exclude points that were within 50 m of shore, or truncate all point counts to a smaller distance?

2.) How does Distance (in either GUI or R form) calculate an estimate for abundance based on the probability of detection? I am ending up with estimates of abundance that seem way too small to be reasonable.

I have tried specifying the entire island area as region area. When I do this, I get really low estimates of abundance for medium and small islands - many of them are just estimated at zero, even ones with 15-20 detections. When I do this, I get really low estimates of abundance on all islands, including large ones - the total of all estimates is ~500 individuals, when I observed ~3500 in the project. Does this have to do with how I'm specifying effort? I have it as 1 per point count. (so an island with 3 point counts would have an effort of 3 overall).

Deb

messages.body_plain:
Hi Irene and Landry,

It may not surprise you to learn that there is no one-size-fits-all answer to your question. If you have two species with similar detectability then a pooled detection function should work fine. But because usually in this situation one or more of the species we want to pool has few detections associated with it, we typically have limited data to show this. This means you are making a judgement call, the validity of which depends on your understanding of the relevant species, habitats, survey methods etc.

That said, it's still worth looking at how distributions for the different species compare with one another. If you see evidence of different detectability even with your limited sample, you should be cautious about using a pooled function. One thing to be aware of, when making these comparisons, is cluster size. I imagine this is an important factor to take account of when estimating detection functions fit monkeys. In which case detectability should ideally be compared between groups of similar size.

Building a detection function just using data for the common species is probably a good idea for estimating densities of the common species. However, I can't think of an advantage of excluding spider monkey data from the detection function aimed at estimating densities of spider monkeys.

Using non-survey spider monkey detections to boost your sample sizes for detection functions is a good idea. Just be careful that the detections in question were made in similar habitats and circumstances, so that adding them to your dataset is valid. For example, if your transects are all along forest tracks, then adding detections from forest edges (where detectability might be greater) or from off-piste ramblings in the forest interior (where detectability might be lower) is likely to be problematic.

Best wishes,

Mark

Hi Debora,

Your study seems quite interesting.

The key aspect I believe you need to consider is how did you select the location of your points within the islands. If the majority of the islands and you always places a point near the center, I can only expect even if everything else was correct you would get very biased estimates, because the density of most species will not be uniform across the islands. Those that prefer the center of the islands would be overestimated, those that prefer the outskirts would be underestimated. So this is a good example of a situation where strong density gradients might be present, and hence you need to consider these from the start - i.e. from the survey design stage - which, if you have not, might render the data extremely hard to analyze.

Regardless, your question regarding estimates of 0 for islands with many detections raises additional warnings. There might be something going fundamentally wrong above and beyond what I mention above. At what level are you making your predictions? You should not really attempt to make predictions at the island level if you only have 1 or 2 points per island. And when you say you included "the area of land within 50 m as effort" - not sure what that means, but that could be the cause for some of the problems. The effort should be 1 for each (time you sampled a) point. Then if you only surveyed say 180 degrees, half a circle, the effort would be 0.5. But if you survey up to w (the truncation distance) in half the circle, and up to w/2 in the other half, there's no simple way to record effort. What you are doing then is changing a fundamental aspect of the distance sampling component - the otherwise triangular distribution of distances that we need to assume for conventional methods to work no longer holds, and while we can still come up with ways of coping with that, no existing software on the shelf will do it - you would probably have to code it yourself.

There are definitely ways that the unequal sampling area could be accounted for, but they are not really straightforward, but as I stated above, my main worry is about density gradients.  I suggest if you want we continue the discussion offline, then if some useful conclusion is reached, you can post it online.

Cheers

T

Hello,

Thank you all for the input. Eric, the dht2 function is exactly what I was looking for, thank you very much! I appreciate you taking time from the distance sampling workshop you are currently at.

Mark, from what I understand the correct use would be your latter scenario (if you are going for species level estimates). If differences between detectability are small between two (or more) similar species, the observations from them can be pooled to get a detection function. There should of course be some kind of evidence or expertise to support that assumption. The dht2 function then provides a straightforward way to use the detection function you estimated from both or multiple species and get species level abundance estimates.

-Landry

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

We surveyed for a species of grassland sparrow this year that is notoriously difficult to see, even if they are singing. The result is that we have detection data for a lot of birds for whom we were unable to get accurate distance data (i.e., we heard the bird but were unable to establish its distance from the survey station).

Let's say we have 200 detections, but only 100 of those had distance data. We analyze the data in Distance and get a density estimate (1.0 bird/ha in this example). But I know that there were additional birds out there that didn't factor into the density analysis, so is there any way to really capture that? Or is that just something that gets explained in the report, without any way of really accounting for those "missing" 100 birds mathematically?

Thanks in advance for the help,

Nick

messages.body_plain:
Sara

You've been busy fitting models, but I think you've probably done more fitting than is necessary.  Post-stratification is used if you want to estimate density of categories of objects and those categories are not known to you at the time the study was designed.  Covariates are used if attributes of objects influence detectability and you wish to incorporate that information into your detection function modelling; most often you still achieve adequate estimates even if these covariates are not included in the modelling.

You indicate that there are large differences in estimates between the various models you have fitted.  Those differences must be taken in the context of the uncertainty in those estimates.  Looking at your model results table, and setting aside analyses 12, 13, 14, 15, and 18, density estimates from the other 14 models range between 5 and 9; but note all have confidence intervals between 3 and 12.  In that lights, I'd say there is not considerable variation in estimates between models.

However, you should use model selection tools and more judicious selection of models to fit to guide you to the best model for your data.  As you note, AIC is supposed to assist in model selection.  You are right to be concerned that most of your delta-AIC values are zero.  This is because when data are altered between models, AICs of those models are not comparable.  Note the column fourth from the left (with what appears to be a funnel at the top).  This is the model filter applied to the data for that analysis.  You will see you have applied 18 different filters to your 19 analyses.  The only analyses that used the same filter is analysis 4 and 5 (that is the reason you have a non-zero delta-AIC for analysis 5).  I'm not sure why you were changing your data filters for almost each analysis.  That should be something that changes very little, some initial investigation of truncation then no more alterations to the data filter among analyses.

The modelling decisions you make are driven by the objectives of your study.  If you have adequate fit of simple models and those inferences suit your objectives, then your analysis has reached its conclusion.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick,

Just a small addition to Eric's suggestion that you might think of using the detections for which you have no distance to estimate encounter rate. As well as the question Eric posed about whether birds detected on call might often be in flight, you also have to consider whether the detection function you estimate from registrations with distance will represent birds you were unable to see. I suspect it won't, but you'll have a better feel for this than me. If these birds are mostly detected further away than the subset of birds you get eyes on (and therefore distance estimates for), applying the detection function to the count of aural-only birds will probably over-estimate the number of birds you missed.

I would suggest trying to assign distances to all registrations. You can get practice at this by estimating distances of all birds detected first by ear (on surveys and at other times too), before you get eyes on them. Those birds you do eventually see will allow you to assess your aural-only distance estimates, which should improve as you get more experience at judging distance by ear.

Cheers,

Mark

Sara

Let me clarify.  If you do not know the location of the types of objects for which you wish to stratify, then use post-stratification.

>From the histograms of your data, it appears that you have only a 1 in 4 chance of seeing objects that are between 7 and 14m from the transect--roughly the same as objects 100m from the transect.  How is this possible?  If the objects seen at 100m are of large sizes, perhaps you might consider filtering your data into types (big and small) and fitting separate detection functions to each--and likely also using different truncation distances for each type.  Is that a plausible explanation for this pattern in your histograms?

The detection function shown in  the figures will result in extremely large estimates of density/abundance because the estimated probability of detection arising from a function of that shape is very small--implying a large proportion of objects are missed.  Let's continue to discuss off of the list, then you can provide your conclusions to the list when the situation is more clear.

messages.body_plain:
With the kind help of Eric Rexstad the problem was solved off-list.
The problem was caused by 2 objects (none of them was listed among those in the error message), where the primary and secondary observers did not agree on the species they had observed. So there were different names in the species field of the database for these objects. Using a query in the Distance program the records not matching the right species name were not included in the dataset sent to R. This caused mismatch in the observations/detections by the two observers.
Just a suggestion to the developers of the 'mrds' package: it would be nice if a data checking routine could be included in the code that would check for such cases and list the right object IDs in the error message.

best wishes
Ainars Aunins
